vignette:
Minh is a 27-year-old Vietnamese American journalist who presents with a PCL-5 score of 64 following a period of sustained physical abuse by a former male romantic partner that ended approximately fourteen months ago. He is currently in a new relationship and works for a mid-sized urban news outlet, a role that requires him to move through the city daily, attend press briefings, and conduct in-person interviews - an environment that has become, for him, a landscape of hidden threat.

The abuse unfolded over nearly two years and escalated gradually. His former partner would strike him without warning - across the face, against the ribs, once throwing him against a kitchen counter so hard that he lost his footing. What made it particularly disorienting was the silence that followed: no explanation, no acknowledgment, just the resumption of ordinary life. Minh learned to read the smallest signals - a delay in a reply, a pause before a door opened - as harbingers of what might come. He was rarely wrong, and that vigilance became the architecture of his days.

Now, when something takes longer than expected - a source who doesn't call back on time, a delayed subway car - Minh finds himself certain that something bad is unfolding, his chest tightening in the same way it did when he would hear footsteps approaching the bedroom. He wakes in the night to check that his apartment door is locked, sometimes two or three times, and even after confirming it, he cannot fully accept that he is safe. This inability to trust reassurance is not stubbornness; it is what the abuse taught him, that safety is always provisional. These beliefs - that people cannot be trusted, that he is fundamentally inadequate for having stayed, that harm can come from anyone - keep his nervous system scanning constantly, which means that ordinary encounters are pre-loaded with threat before they begin.

It is the memory itself that most insistently feeds this worldview. When it returns - and it returns without invitation - it does not feel historical. Minh describes it as happening now, in the room, in his body. He feels physical pain in his ribs and jaw, the same locations where he was struck, and the emotional overwhelm is so total that he has had to step away from his desk mid-story, unable to continue. These intrusions do not leave him thinking about the past; they confirm, in the present tense, that he is the kind of person to whom this happens, and that the world is the kind of place where it does. The memory thus continuously refreshes his conviction that he is inadequate and that no one can be trusted - and those convictions in turn make the world feel perpetually unsafe, sustaining a vigilance that makes it harder for the memories to recede.

Riding the bus to assignments, Minh sits near the exit and watches the other passengers. Being alone with men - in an elevator, in a waiting room, in the back of a rideshare - produces an acute alertness that he cannot reason his way out of, even when the situation is mundane. When these moments arrive, or when a trauma-related event surfaces in his reporting - a story about domestic violence, a photograph of a bruised face - the memories flood back with particular force. In response, Minh has developed a set of habits that feel like self-protection. He dwells obsessively on what he did wrong in the relationship, replaying choices as though understanding them might inoculate him against repetition. He suppresses any anger he feels, afraid that expressing it would make him dangerous or make him like his former partner. He has begun restricting what he eats, a behaviour he cannot fully explain but that feels like control over the one thing that remains his. These strategies, however, have quietly deepened his sense of himself as broken and unworthy, reinforcing the very beliefs they were meant to quiet.

What finally brought Minh to seek help was a moment at work three weeks ago. He was interviewing a male official in a small conference room and found himself unable to speak - his body had decided, without consulting him, that he was back in that kitchen. His editor noticed. Minh is afraid, above all, that he will never feel safe in his own body again. What he hopes for, tentatively, is that the past might one day feel like the past.
